lines.text: He looked like someone you could trust.
That was part of what made Ted Bundy so frightening.
In the early 1970s, Bundy was a university student in Washington state.
He seemed intelligent and charming.
But behind that image, young women began disappearing.
In 1974, attacks in the Pacific Northwest sparked fear.
Witnesses described a polite, clean-cut man who sometimes pretended to need help.
Investigators struggled to connect the cases as Bundy moved between states.
In 1975, he was arrested in Utah after police stopped his Volkswagen Beetle.
Evidence linked him to crimes, and he was convicted of kidnapping.
But the story was far from over.
In 1977, Bundy escaped custody twice in Colorado.
He eventually reached Florida, where, in January 1978, he attacked a sorority house, killing two young women.
Weeks later, he was arrested in Pensacola.
His trials became a national spectacle.
Bundy sometimes represented himself, turning the courtroom into a stage.
In 1979, he was convicted of the sorority house murders.
In 1989, Bundy was executed in Florida.
His case left a disturbing question.
How could someone hide extreme violence behind an ordinary public image?
Charm is not proof of character.
Appearances never tell the whole story.
